table.text: The following considers a group-level one-sample t test on per-subject contrasts (equivalently, a paired t test of the two percept-conditional means across subjects), with the trial-level effect size fixed at d = ∆/σ = 0.5, where ∆ is the common effect and σ 2 the trial-level (within-subject) variance. The inferential target is a continuous secondary measure (e.g., BOLD amplitude or band power). For each subject we form the per-condition contrast D between the classifier-inferred percepts and test at the group level whether E[ D] differs from zero. Classification accuracy enters as a factor that attenuates the signal and inflates its variance. The derivation (see Appendix) rests on the following assumptions: 1. balanced classes (P (y = 0) ≈ P (y = 1) = 0.5); 2. conditional on the percept the trial-level responses are Gaussian with equal, constant variance σ 2 ; 3. to a first we assume that z t based classification errors are independent of the neural measurement x t, occurring with probability 1 -a where a is the classification accuracy; 4. independent trials (relaxed below for continuous viewing extension below); 5. a common effect ∆ across subjects (relaxed below to allow between-subject variability).

The between-subject term (2 a -1) 2 τ² /4 is independent of m, so power saturates as the trial count grows: adding trials cannot average away variability that lives between subjects. In the large-trial limit λ → √ n ∆/τ, which does not depend on a. In practice this means that once between-subject variance dominates, neither more trials nor higher classification accuracy raise power, only additional subjects do. The heterogeneity τ can be estimated from the between-subject spread of per-subject effect sizes in pilot or active report data. Figure 4b plots Equation ( 2); the resulting saturation is visible as a flattening of the high-trial curves and an upward shift in the accuracy needed to reach a given power relative to the τ = 0 bound.

For a practical example, a BOLD no-report study can be considered where the following parameters are read directly from a pilot recording: session length T = 20 min = 1200 s, sampling rate f s = 1 Hz (so m = T f s = 1200 samples), mean dominance duration tdom = 6 s, trial-level noise SD σ = 1, and a residual-noise correlation time of t noise = 2 s estimated from the autocorrelation of the percept-removed residual. The effect size, between subject SD and classification accuracy have a relatively large effect on the power estimate, meaning conservative values should be used and sensitivity to small changes should be considered. We use a per-trial standardized effect d = 0.5, between-subject SD τ = 0.2, and a classification accuracy a = 0.70 (deflated from a cross-validated pilot value of 0.75).

Evaluating the exact noncentral-t power (possible using the functions provided in the script available onlinefoot_2 ; see "required_n_2comp" function) corrects this upward, because at such small n the critical value is well above the normal quantile: power is 0.766 at n = 6 and 0.855 at n = 7, meaning the required sample size for this example would be at least n = 7.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Ambiguous, multistable stimuli can give rise to multiple perceptual interpretations.
Bistable visual stimuli, in particular, have long been used to study neural and cognitive processes.

However, many experimental paradigms rely on self-report to assess subjective perceptual experiences, introducing potential issues such as low reliability and interferences of reporting into the processes under investigation.
No-report paradigms serve as a method to work around these problems by decoding perceptual content based on physiological or neural data.
Here we discuss the strengths and pitfalls of no-report paradigms in the context of research using multistable perception.
Focusing on experimental power related to decoding accuracy, we illustrate current progress of decoding perceptual content using three major data modalities (eye tracking, M/EEG and fMRI).
We find that the predictability of the percept varies significantly depending on the paradigm and stimulus type.

Finally, we introduce a method and open-source toolkit to calculate experimental power to plan future no-report studies, accounting for limited classification accuracy when decoding perceptual states.

text.text: Experimental participants who view these ambiguous stimuli often experience a bistable (multistable) percept, with the stimuli alternating between two (or more) perceptual states over time.
Visual bistability has been central to a wide range of research questions spanning both cognitive and neural domains.

Aside from being studied extensively itself (e.g., Blake & Logothetis, 2002; Kruse & Stadler, 1995; Leopold & Logothetis, 1999; Levelt, 1965), neural activity related to alternations between the two perceptual states has yielded significant insights into perceptual organization (e.g., Hohwy et al., 2008; Schmack et al., 2016) as well as feature binding and information integration (e.g., Canales-Johnson et al., 2023; Haynes & Rees, 2005; Rose & Büchel, 2005; Tsuchiya et al., 2015).

text.text: In this paper, we review the findings that contribute to the development of the two stages of no-report paradigms in bistable perception, namely the development of a classification pipeline (primary analysis) and the adaptation of this pipeline to investigate processes isolated from report (secondary analysis).
We then provide recommendations to authors wanting to conduct studies involving visual multistability for topics in psychology and cognitive neuroscience.

Finally, we propose a method to calculate experimental power to plan future no-report studies, specifically accounting for power attenuation due to imperfect classification in the decoding stage of no-report paradigms.

text.text: But even if one regards perceptual content as synonymous with what participants are able to report, several issues remain.
We identify three key issues with the reliance on active report in studies of multistable perception.

As active report engages various cognitive and physiological processes, a key challenge in studies aiming to isolate the neural correlates of perception is their separation from activity associated with active report.

Specifically, active report involves moderators such as attention, post-perceptual processes such as working memory and decision making, and may engage downstream processes such as metacognition (Block, 2019; Cohen et al., 2020; Duman et al., 2022).

Active report generally serves as ground truth to determine the occurrence of perceptual alternations.
However, it is a delayed measure (the report is always later than the transition itself), and it is not straightforward to estimate the temporal precision of the response directly.
Certain physiological measures are known to be more tightly linked to stimulus features and therefore provide an indirect estimate of the temporal precision of active report.

No-report paradigms are experimental designs in consciousness and perception science that aim to infer a person's subjective experience without requiring explicit behavioral report (or more general decision-making), such as button presses or verbal responses.

By excluding interfering and confounding processes related to active report, some authors have argued that these experimental setups have the potential for more valid and reliable insights into the underlying neural mechanisms of conscious experience (Block, 2019; Cohen et al., 2020; Pitts, Metzler, & Hillyard, 2014; Tsuchiya et al., 2015) and no-report task versions have been used in a range of experimental setups, including visual masking, auditory detection, dichoptic fusion and multistable perception paradigms (e.g., Alilović et al., 2023; Cohen et al., 2020 Cohen et al., , 2024;; Fahrenfort et al., 2012; Frässle et al., 2014; Hatamimajoumerd et al., 2022; Hesse & Tsao, 2020; Pitts, Metzler, & Hillyard, 2014).

text.text: In simple masking or detection-type paradigms, one can directly compare report and no-report conditions by presenting the same stimuli in different blocks, one in which the participant is asked for a response and one in which it is not, and then comparing the observed neural signals.

In multistable perception tasks (e.g., binocular rivalry), however, one does not know when the percept changes during no-report trials, because conditions (e.g., seeing a house or a face) are inferred post hoc based on reports of the participant.

Therefore, no-report studies of multistable perception mostly follow a similar two-step structure, starting with the establishment of an indirect marker of perceptual switches during a report session (e.g., eye movements, optokinetic nystagmus, pupil size, neural measures) to classify perceptual alternations (primary analysis; see left panel of Figure 2).

text.text: Specifically, since the conditions under which features are recorded differ between report and no-report conditions, the set of features that is used to set up a classifier is different from the set of features which the classifier is applied to.
This means that it is not straightforward to assess the classifier's accuracy, making it difficult to validate the classification of no-report trials.

Given that a valid and reliable classification of perceptual content is central to the success of no-report studies using multistable perception, in the following, we review the current progress and methods that allow or could allow for accurate classification of perceptual content in multistable perception paradigms.
We emphasize the importance of establishing validity when establishing a classification pipeline and discuss several possibilities to achieve and evaluate validity.
We divide classification possibilities by the type of physiological measurement taken, starting with eye tracking followed by M/EEG and fMRI.

Since many studies do not employ classifiers with easy-to-calculate classification accuracies, we highlight the role of studies finding condition differences between perceptual phases and to what extent these insights could serve as a foundation for classification in future no-report studies.
Finally, we present a method to assess the expected power in no-report studies using bistable perception given an expected classification accuracy.
Overall, the discussed aspects together with the methodology to calculate power should provide a useful guide to plan successful no-report studies.
Successful classification of perceptual content depends on the effect size of a condition difference between two percepts.

When it comes to the classification of momentary percepts in bistable perception paradigms, previous literature can be divided into studies that perform prediction, allowing for a more direct estimate of a classification accuracy, and studies that recover condition differences relating to specific percepts.

While the first delivers direct insights for future no-report studies, the second can still give an indication of an implied classification accuracy assuming an effect size can be derived from published statistics.

Specifically, an estimate of the effect size (e.g., Cohen's d) can often be calculated from test statistics or through reported means and variance (Rosnow & Rosenthal, 2003), which translates to an effect size in a possible classification scenario (Rice & Harris, 2005).

Paired with the parallel movement of the eyes, the physical separation of input streams in binocular rivalry has allowed the development of consistent methodologies to infer cognitive processes based on eye response.
Especially approaches using luminance-induced pupil dilation or optokinetic nystagmus have shown high classification accuracy (see next section).
On the other end of the spectrum are static ambiguous figures where prediction of perceptual content seems to be more difficult.

Optokinetic nystagmus (OKN) is a reflexive eye movement that occurs when viewing a moving visual scene, consisting of a slow tracking (pursuit) phase in the direction of motion followed by a quick saccadic reset in the opposite direction.
It helps stabilize the visual field on the retina and is commonly used to assess motion perception and visual function (Hale et al., 2024; Kang et al., 2023; Reinecke, 1961).

text.text: In the case of binocular rivalry, two gratings continuously moving in opposite directions can be presented to each eye while tracking eye movements.
Because of parallel eye movements, the smooth pursuit phase of the OKN typically aligns with the motion direction of the dominant percept (i.e., one of the two gratings).

OKN has been found to be a robust correlate of reported percepts, and is successfully used as basis for the classification of percepts in binocular rivalry setups (Aleshin et al., 2019; Enoksson, 1963; Fox et al., 1975; Wei & Sun, 1998).

text.text: This is especially useful for binocular rivalry paradigms, enabling the presentation of differently luminous stimuli to each eye.
Since the pupillary response is typically symmetrical, both pupils tend to respond corresponding to the luminance of the currently attended stimulus.

In practice, with one brighter and one darker stimulus present, the viewer's pupil tends to constrict when the brighter stimulus dominates perception and vice versa (Binda et al., 2013; Mathot et al., 2014; Mathôt et al., 2013; Naber et al., 2011).

text.text: They found that participants who were instructed to sustain an initially primed perspective of a Necker cube and experienced no perceptual shift after stimulus onset, had, on-average, larger changes in pupil diameter when seeing the cube from the above-perspective compared to seeing the cube from a below-perspective.
However, they found no such effect for a passive viewing condition or in a separate experiment where the cubes were rotated to be perceived sideways.
The authors presume that differences in pupil dilation within the experiments reflect perceptual content (i.e., seeing the cube from above vs from below) rather than perceptual reversals.

The success of classifying perceptual states and perceptual reversals based on eye-tracking data depends strongly on the experimental paradigm and the concrete measure that is taken.

Binocular rivalry allows for very accurate prediction using OKN and luminance-based pupil dilation, given any setup that provokes differential behavior between the two stimuli (Frässle et al., 2014; Fujiwara et al., 2017; Leopold et al., 1995; Naber et al., 2011).

text.text: Many approaches show promising correlates between perception and eye-behavior such as arousal-related pupil-dilation, microsaccades, eye-movement or blinks, but the signal strength of these effects (and thus likely individual effect sizes) has been found to be small.

Still, while these signals might not be strong enough to serve as accurate predictors for perception on their own for real-time prediction, they could possibly be combined for a more elaborate prediction model.

Since all of these measures can be easily extracted from a single eye-tracking session, combining features based on pupil dilation, microsaccades and other eye-movement data could result in higher classification accuracies.
Electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) are non-invasive methods that can follow neural dynamics at the sub-second timescale.
EEG records voltage changes produced by synchronous post-synaptic activity and routinely resolves events with millisecond precision, albeit at the cost of reduced spatial detail.

MEG captures the accompanying magnetic fields, which are less distorted by tissue conductivity (though they can be distorted by source-to-sensor distance; Srinivasan et al., 2007) while retaining comparable temporal acuity.
text.formatted: MEG captures the accompanying magnetic fields, which are less distorted by tissue conductivity (though they can be distorted by source-to-sensor distance; <ref type="bibr" target="#b157">Srinivasan et al., 2007)</ref> while retaining comparable temporal acuity.

text.text: The two main approaches to decode perceptual alternations using EEG and MEG can be summarized as methods based on event-related potentials (ERPs) and methods based on steady-state visually evoked potentials (SSVEPs).

ERPs consist of positive or negative voltage deflections that occur in the EEG trace following discrete events such as the onset of a visual stimulus, a motor response, or a spontaneous perceptual reversal in an ambiguous figure.

SSVEPs, on the other hand, are oscillatory responses that are phase-locked to periodic visual stimulation: when a display flickers at a constant frequency, that frequency (and its harmonics) is reflected in the visual cortex, yielding a steady-state signal that can be used to "tag" and continuously track the dominance of competing percepts without requiring overt reports.
As signatures of cognitive processes, ERPs have potential as predictors for certain mental states or task-related intentions.
Especially in the context of brain-computer interfaces, they can be leveraged to decode user intent in real time (Abiri et al., 2019; Wolpaw, 2013).
text.formatted: Especially in the context of brain-computer interfaces, they can be leveraged to decode user intent in real time <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abiri et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b178">Wolpaw, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Typically, reliable decoding leverages specific pre-extracted ERP features such as mean amplitudes within time-windows or spatial topographies, fed into machine learning models (e.g., support-vector machines, SVMs) trained for each individual and task.
Although in many no-report studies, M/EEG signals are treated as the dependent variable, there are some indications that classification of percepts based on them might be feasible.
In the case of ERPs, detection of percept related signatures usually revolves around events such as perceptual reversals or stimulus onsets.
Due to the weak neural signatures of perceptual reversals themselves, it often takes trial-averaging to detect them in the first place.

Further, as a measure with relatively low spatial resolution, it is especially difficult to disentangle signals resulting from report-related processes and percept related processes when training a classifier.
Given this, the possible application of M/EEG to provide features for no-report classification might be limited.
Still, some relatively recent studies successfully developed classification pipelines to decode perceptual content based on M/EEG.
In the case of binocular rivalry, stimulus content can be leveraged to decode perception.
Especially the perception of faces is associated with distinct ERPs such as the N170 and the P2 (Rossion & Caharel, 2011).

text.text: In an MEG study, Sandberg et al. (2013) leveraged the distinct signatures related to face perception by setting up a trial-by-trial binocular rivalry paradigm with faces presented to one eye and gratings presented to the other eye.
text.formatted: In an MEG study, <ref type="bibr" target="#b151">Sandberg et al. (2013)</ref> leveraged the distinct signatures related to face perception by setting up a trial-by-trial binocular rivalry paradigm with faces presented to one eye and gratings presented to the other eye.

text.text: A support-vector machine was trained to classify each time-point within a trial for classification of face vs grating perception (both within-subject and between-subject).
For time points that matched the timing of face-related ERPs, across trial-averaged prediction accuracy was as high as 90%.
The highest prediction accuracy was achieved by combining readings from all sensors, with occipital readings likely contributing the most.
These results indicate that given the right features, a classification algorithm for entire trials could possibly result in high-accuracy prediction of binocular rivalry percepts using EEG or MEG.

Steady-state visually evoked potentials (SSVEPs), or so-called frequency tagging methods, are an oft-used tool in M/EEG research.

By exciting the retina through visual stimulation with a certain frequency (e.g., a flickering target stimulus during an experiment), corresponding cortical activities observed in M/EEG reflect this induced frequency and/or multiples of it (Norcia et al., 2015; Regan, 1977).

(2024) found a near-perfect correlation between self-reported percept changes and estimates based on frequency tagging of the different stimuli.
They however found no significant correlation between average estimated reversal-rates from a no-report condition and the average reversal-rates in the self report condition.

While the authors explain this with attentional differences between the two conditions, the missing correlation does not support the validity of frequency tagging as a method to infer perceptual states in no-report paradigms.

text.text: As of now, the usability of M/EEG to reliably classify transient conscious percepts in multistable perception paradigms is somewhat limited.
If viewing paradigms are split into single trials, ERPs can be decoded to classify percepts relatively reliably.
SSVEPs on the other hand seem to be more suitable to classify perceptual stability and perceptual reversals in prolonged viewing paradigms.
Both approaches are highly stimulus dependent, with binocular rivalry and stimuli involving the viewing of human faces being the easiest to decode (Parkkonen et al., 2008).

For example, OKN and SSVEP responses track stimulus content.

text.text: To ensure a valid classification on no-report data, the utilized feature sets of report and no-report data should not differ.

text.text: In practice, developing a discriminator to classify data from these feature sets as belonging to "report" and "no-report" categories should result in low accuracy (as the feature is present in both conditions).
A high classification accuracy here can indicate a significant portion of report-related signals in the feature set of the report data (as the feature is only present in the report condition).
If this is the case, there is a higher chance of a no-report classification model relying on these purely report related signals.
However, as these signals are missing in the feature set of no-report data, the no-report classification for a primary analysis is less likely to succeed.

A more ambitious extension would train the decoder in an unsupervised manner on no-report data in which the percept itself is uncertain (e.g., ambiguous or masked stimuli) and then validate it against report labels.
This is likely a harder problem, since uncertainty would concern not only the timing but also the identity of the percept, which decreases the chances of finding a valid decision boundary.
Still, if successfully validated on report data, this method could provide one of the most valid approaches to classify perceptual content in no-report paradigms.

text.text: To plan a study using the tools described above, estimates for the expected standardized per-trial effect size, between subject variability, and classification accuracy are needed.
For the extension to the continuous case, an estimate for the average dominance duration and the autocorrelation of the measurement noise are necessary.

Values for the classification accuracy a, average dominance duration tdom , residual-noise correlation time t noise (residuals within dominance periods), and within subject variability σ can be estimated from an active report pilot study.
Due to the domain shift, classification accuracy derived from an active report pilot should be seen as an optimistic upper bound.
The trial standardized effect size d of the secondary measure and the between subject variability τ are more difficult to estimate.
Since τ is a feature of the effect size distribution, and any estimate on a low n pilot would be very imprecise, it is best to use a conservative estimate.

In this paper, we identified two-stages in the study of perceptual rivalry in no-report paradigms: a primary analysis to classify distinct perceptual phases and a secondary analysis to establish an effect independent of report-related processes.
We reviewed the current research on (possible) physiological predictors of perceptual (rivalrous) phases and discussed the usefulness and validity of certain measures and features.

Further, we provided a method to determine statistical power of the secondary analysis assuming an established classification accuracy in the primary analysis and listed possible pitfalls to avoid in future no-report studies involving bistable perception.

Generally, we find that the effectiveness of physiological measures as predictors for bistable percepts varies markedly: some -most notably those harnessing optokinetic nystagmus (OKN) during binocular rivalry -achieve near-perfect correspondence with self-report and may even outperform report when lapses in responses are considered.
Others however, barely exceed chance level and are therefore less suitable, especially when statistical power cannot be improved by increasing the number of participant or trials.
Binocular rivalry seems to provide the richest diagnostic signals, because the conflicting monocular inputs elicit robust reflexive responses.

Regarding this, the most successful analysis pipelines embed stimulus features that drive involuntary oculomotor or autonomic reactions, such as motion-induced OKN or luminance-dependent pupil dilation.

Static ambiguous figures, by contrast, offer few stimulus-locked physiological features and thus yield the poorest accuracy, whereas dynamic ambiguous stimuli, in particular the moving plaid, currently afford reliable eye-tracking-based classification, especially taking into account that accuracy has shown to improve further when neural measures (e.g., multivoxel fMRI patterns) are added to the feature set (Wilbertz et al., 2018).

text.text: Classifier performance is shaped by an interaction between stimulus class and measurement modality.
For example, for EEG/ERP-based setups, the classification of perceptual reversals is difficult.
This is mostly due to the low signal to noise ratio and the short duration of event-related components related to reversals.

Nonetheless, in trial-based setups, EEG reveals clear correlates to perceptual states (Kornmeier & Bach, 2012), which possibly could be leveraged for more elaborate classifiers in continuous viewing paradigms in the future when analysis methods advance.

text.text: Overall, matching specific measurement approaches to stimulus characteristics, and combining several measurement approaches, offers great opportunity for tracking perceptual states without having to rely on overt reports.
Based on the power analysis tool we proposed, we can note a few main aspects.
Firstly, misclassification shrinks the usable effect by a factor of (2a -1), so a drop in accuracy a from 0.9 to 0.7 roughly halves it.
Secondly, between-subject variability limits the power that can be achieved through more trials or better classifiers.

Finally, for continuous viewing, the number of expected dominance durations can be used as a accurate shorthand for the effective trial counts (for slower measures like BOLD, it is somewhat conservative).
Generally, we recommend conservative estimates as inputs for the tool to rule out underpowered designs.

We hope that the practical recommendations presented here help make multistable perception paradigms even more powerful tools for studying the neural correlates and mechanisms of conscious perception, and ultimately for testing competing theories of consciousness.
